title: Jajangmyeon
description: Thick wheat noodles piled with a glossy, faintly sweet black bean and pork sauce — the everyday lunch order from every Korean-Chinese restaurant and a certified kids' favorite.

ingredients.item: potato, peeled and cut into 1cm cubes

steps: Stir-fry the pork belly in a wok with 1 tablespoon vegetable oil over high heat for 4-5 minutes until golden and crisp, then drain off excess fat.
Add the radish and stir-fry 1 minute, then add the potato, onion and zucchini and keep stirring 3 minutes until the potato turns translucent at the edges.
Push the vegetables to the side, add the remaining oil and the chunjang to the cleared center, and fry the paste alone for 1 minute before stirring everything together.
Pour in the water, cover, and simmer 10 minutes until the radish and potato are fully tender.
Stir in the starch slurry a little at a time until the sauce turns glossy and thick, then stir in the sesame oil and remove from the heat.
Boil the noodles in a large pot until chewy, drain, rinse under cold water, and divide among 4 bowls.
Ladle the sauce generously over the noodles and top with cucumber matchsticks; serve immediately with kimchi or pickled radish.
tips: Fry the chunjang paste alone in oil before mixing it in — this step removes its raw bitterness and is the difference between good and great jjajangmyeon.
Toss the noodles with a little sesame oil if not serving immediately so they don't clump together.
nutritionNote: Rich in refined carbs and pork fat with modest vegetables; balance with a side of cucumber or radish kimchi and go light on extra starch slurry to keep sodium in check.

title: Jjamppong
description: A fiery, briny seafood noodle soup in a bright red anchovy broth loaded with mussels, shrimp, squid and vegetables — the fire-breathing cousin of jajangmyeon from Korea's Chinese restaurants.

ingredients.item: fresh jjajangmyeon noodles (thick wheat noodles), thawed if frozen
dried anchovies, heads and guts removed
thinly sliced pork, cut into bite-size pieces
napa cabbage, cut into bite-size pieces

steps: Combine the anchovies, kelp and water in a large pot; boil 20 minutes covered, then 20 minutes more uncovered over low heat, then strain and reserve the stock.
Heat the vegetable oil in a wok over high heat and stir-fry the garlic, pork and vegetables for 2-3 minutes until the pork is no longer pink.
Stir in the gochugaru and fry 1 minute until the oil turns deep red and fragrant.
Pour in the reserved stock, bring to a boil, then add the mussels, shrimp and squid and simmer 5 minutes until the seafood is just cooked through.
Season with the fish sauce and salt to taste.
Boil the noodles separately until chewy, drain, and divide among 4 deep bowls.
Ladle the boiling seafood broth and toppings over the noodles and serve immediately, steaming hot.
tips: Don't overcook the mussels, shrimp and squid or they turn rubbery — add them last and pull the pot off the heat the moment they're opaque.
For a milder family batch, swap half the gochugaru for sweet paprika; the color stays deep red but the heat drops sharply.
kidNote: Ladle the kids' portions from a milder batch made with half gochugaru swapped for paprika, or serve plain noodles with a spoonful of broth and a few mild shrimp and vegetables picked out before the chile flakes go in.
nutritionNote: High in sodium from the anchovy stock and fish sauce and quite spicy; balance with steamed rice and go easy on refilling the broth, which carries most of the salt.

title: Kalguksu
description: A clean, comforting noodle soup of hand-cut wheat noodles simmered in anchovy broth with clams, prawns and julienned vegetables — Korea's answer to chicken soup on a rainy day.

ingredients.item: knife-cut noodles (kalguksu noodles), store-bought or homemade

steps: Bring the anchovy and kelp stock to a boil, then stir in the soy sauce, garlic and salt.
Add the zucchini, carrot and shiitake mushrooms and cook 2 minutes until just softened.
Add the clams and prawns and boil another 2 minutes until just cooked through; do not overcook or the seafood turns tough.
Meanwhile, boil the noodles in a separate pot for 2-3 minutes until cooked, then drain and rinse under cold water.
Add the noodles to the soup pot and simmer 1 minute to warm through, stirring gently.
Scatter over the green onion, turn off the heat, and ladle into bowls to serve hot.
tips: Buy pre-cut kalguksu noodles from a Korean grocery to skip the hour of hand-cutting dough.
Keep the broth at a bare simmer once the seafood goes in so the clams and prawns stay tender.
nutritionNote: A light broth-based meal that's high in sodium from the anchovy stock and soy sauce; add extra zucchini and carrot for fibre and rinse the clams well to control saltiness.

title: Janchi Guksu
description: Thin wheat noodles in a savory anchovy broth topped with silky egg strips and vegetables — the 'banquet noodles' Koreans serve at weddings and birthdays to wish for a long life.

ingredients.item: green onion, white and pale green part

steps: Make an egg omelette by cooking the beaten eggs thinly in an oiled pan; roll, cool, and slice into thin strips for garnish.
In the same pan, quickly stir-fry the zucchini and carrot separately with a pinch of salt until just wilted; set aside with the egg strips.
Bring the anchovy and kelp stock to a boil with the green onion and onion; season with the soy sauce and salt, then keep hot.
Boil the somyeon noodles in a separate pot for 2-3 minutes until just tender, then drain and rinse well under cold water to remove excess starch.
Divide the noodles among 4 bowls and ladle the hot stock over them.
Top each bowl with the egg strips, zucchini and carrot, and serve the seasoning sauce on the side for guests to add themselves.
tips: Rinse the boiled noodles thoroughly in cold water — this washes off the surface starch that would otherwise cloud and thicken the broth.
Keep the stock and noodles separate until the moment of serving so the noodles stay springy instead of going soft.
nutritionNote: Light and low in fat, built around broth and noodles; add extra egg and vegetable toppings to the kids' bowls to round out the protein.

title: Kongguksu
description: Chilled wheat noodles bathed in nutty, ice-cold soy milk with cucumber, egg and tomato — a dairy-free, protein-rich noodle soup Koreans crave through the hottest days of summer.

ingredients.item: dried soybeans, soaked in cold water overnight

steps: Drain the soaked soybeans and simmer in the cooking water for 15 minutes uncovered, then cover and simmer 5 minutes more over low heat; cool 10 minutes.
Transfer the beans with about a cup of their cooking water to a blender, add the cold water, sesame seeds and pine nuts, and blend 1-2 minutes until completely smooth and creamy.
Chill the soy milk in an airtight container for at least 1 hour, up to 24 hours.
Boil the somyeon noodles 2-3 minutes until tender, then drain and rinse repeatedly in cold water, rubbing gently between your palms until cold and no longer slippery.
Divide the noodles among 4 bowls, stir the salt into the chilled soy milk, and pour it over the noodles.
Top with cucumber matchsticks, egg wedges and tomato, add ice cubes if you like, and serve immediately with a side of kimchi.
tips: A high-powered blender gives the smoothest, least grainy soy milk — strain through a fine sieve if yours leaves the milk gritty.
Make the soy milk a day ahead; the flavor deepens and it's already cold for serving.
nutritionNote: A plant-protein-rich, dairy-free dish that's naturally low in sodium before you add salt to taste; balance with a protein side if serving as a light lunch.

title: Gimbap
description: Seasoned rice, egg, pickled radish, carrot and ham rolled tight in toasted seaweed and sliced into bite-size wheels — Korea's classic picnic and packed-lunch roll.

ingredients.item: yellow radish pickle (danmuji), cut into strips

steps: Parboil the spinach 30 seconds, rinse in cold water, squeeze dry, and season with a pinch of salt and a little sesame oil.
Cook the beaten eggs into a thin omelette in an oiled pan, then slice into long strips.
In the same pan, briefly stir-fry the carrot, crab sticks and ham separately over medium heat, about 1 minute each.
Mix the warm rice with the remaining sesame oil and salt.
Lay a seaweed sheet shiny-side down on a bamboo mat, spread a thin, even layer of rice over two-thirds of it, leaving a 2-inch gap at the top.
Arrange the danmuji, ham, crab stick, egg strips, carrot and spinach in a line across the rice, then roll tightly using the mat, sealing the edge with a little water.
Repeat with the remaining sheets and fillings, brush the outside of each roll lightly with sesame oil, and slice into bite-size pieces with a sharp, damp knife.
tips: Season the rice while it's still warm so the sesame oil and salt absorb evenly, but let it cool slightly before rolling or the seaweed will steam and go chewy.
Wipe the knife blade with a damp cloth between cuts for clean slices.
nutritionNote: A balanced grab-and-go meal with rice, egg and vegetables; go light on the ham and add extra cucumber or lettuce strips for more fibre.

title: Pan-Fried Pork Dumplings
description: Pork, beef, tofu and chive dumplings pan-fried until the wrapper crisps and the bottom turns deep gold — a family dumpling-folding project that ends in a stack of dippable, golden pockets.
steps: Mix the ground pork and beef with the salt, sesame oil and a pinch of pepper in a large bowl.
Toss the chopped chives with a little oil so they don't wilt, then mix them in with the meat along with the chopped shiitake, onion, soy sauce and sugar.
Squeeze the tofu dry, season with a pinch of salt and sesame oil, and fold it and the garlic into the filling until evenly combined.
Place a spoonful of filling in the center of a wrapper, wet one edge with water, fold in half, and press the edges together to seal.
Heat the vegetable oil in a nonstick pan over medium heat and arrange the dumplings in a single layer.
Cover and cook 3-4 minutes, then flip, add 2-3 tablespoons of water, cover again, and steam-fry 3-4 minutes more until the wrappers are translucent and the bottoms are golden.
Uncover and cook 1 minute more to crisp the bottoms, then transfer to a plate.
Mix the soy sauce and vinegar for the dipping sauce and serve alongside the hot dumplings.
tips: Squeeze the chives and tofu as dry as possible — excess moisture is the main reason homemade mandu filling turns watery and tears the wrappers.
Freeze extra shaped dumplings on a tray before bagging them; they fry from frozen with a couple of extra minutes covered.
nutritionNote: A protein-dense dumpling that's pan-fried in oil; balance the meal with a side of cold seasoned spinach or a cucumber salad and go light on the dipping sauce for sodium.

title: Hotteok
description: Chewy, yeasted street-cart pancakes stuffed with molten brown sugar, cinnamon and toasted seeds, pan-fried until the crust crackles — Korea's favorite cold-weather sweet snack.

ingredients.item: roasted mixed seeds and nuts, chopped

steps: Dissolve the yeast and 1 teaspoon of the sugar in the warm milk and let it foam for 5 minutes.
Whisk the flour, sweet rice flour, salt and remaining sugar together, then stir in the yeast mixture and oil to form a soft, sticky dough.
Cover and let the dough rise in a warm spot for about 1 hour, until doubled in size.
Mix the brown sugar, cinnamon and chopped seeds and nuts together for the filling.
Oil your hands, pinch off a portion of dough, flatten it into a disc, and spoon filling into the center; gather the edges up and pinch to seal into a ball.
Heat a lightly oiled griddle over medium heat, place a dough ball seam-side down, and press it flat with an oiled spatula into a thick disc.
Pan-fry 2-3 minutes per side until deep golden brown, pressing occasionally so the sugar filling melts evenly without bursting through.
Let cool for a minute before serving — the filling is molten straight off the griddle.
tips: Let the sugar filling cool for a full minute before you bite in; it turns lava-hot the instant it melts.
Oil your hands and the spatula generously — the dough is sticky and this keeps it from tearing when you seal and flatten it.
The dough's 1-hour rise is unattended time on top of the active prep and cook minutes listed.
nutritionNote: A sugar-and-fried-dough treat best kept to a once-in-a-while snack; the nuts and seeds add some fibre and healthy fat but don't offset the sugar, so pair with fruit rather than a second helping.

title: Yachaejeon
description: A crisp, savory pancake of julienned zucchini, onion, sweet potato and chili in a light batter fried into one big golden disc — the rainy-day snack every Korean grandmother has on rotation.
steps: Mix the soy sauce, vinegar, gochugaru and sesame seeds in a small bowl for the dipping sauce and set aside.
Combine the green onions, leek, zucchini, chili, onion and sweet potato in a large bowl.
Add the flour, salt and water to the vegetables and mix with a wooden spoon into a loose batter.
Heat a large nonstick skillet over medium-high heat, add 2 tablespoons of oil, and pour in the batter, spreading it into a thin, even layer.
Turn the heat to medium, press the sliced mushroom on top, and cook 4-5 minutes until the bottom is crisp and light golden, swirling the pan occasionally for even cooking.
Flip the pancake, raise the heat to medium-high, and drizzle 1-2 tablespoons of oil around the edges so it runs underneath.
Cook 3-4 minutes more until deeply golden and crisp on both sides, then slide onto a cutting board.
Cut into wedges and serve hot with the dipping sauce.
tips: Slice everything into thin, matchstick-sized pieces so the vegetables cook through in the same time as the batter crisps.
Skip cucumber in the mix — its water content makes the pancake soggy instead of crisp.
nutritionNote: A vegetable-forward, meat-free dish that's pan-fried in oil; blot briefly on a paper towel and pair with a protein side to round out the meal.

title: Dak-kkochi
description: Skewered chicken thigh grilled until charred at the edges, then brushed with a sticky-sweet gochujang glaze — the smoky, chewy chicken-on-a-stick sold from every Korean night market cart.

ingredients.item: boneless chicken thighs, cut into 4cm pieces

steps: Combine the chicken with the soy sauce, black pepper, garlic and green onion; cover and marinate in the fridge at least 30 minutes, up to overnight.
Mix the gochujang, rice syrup, gochugaru, vinegar, oil and water into a smooth, shiny sauce; set aside.
Thread the marinated chicken onto soaked wooden skewers, alternating with rice cake pieces if using.
Grill the skewers over medium heat, or in a hot cast-iron grill pan on the stovetop, for about 5 minutes per side until the chicken is cooked through.
Brush the red sauce generously over both sides and cook 1-2 minutes more, turning once, until the sauce is glossy and slightly caramelized.
Remove from the heat and serve immediately, with extra sauce on the side.
tips: Soak wooden skewers in cold water for 30 minutes before threading so they don't scorch on the grill.
Brush the sauce on only in the last few minutes — its sugar content will burn if it hits the heat too early.
The 30-minute marinade is unattended time on top of the active prep and cook minutes listed.
kidNote: Set aside a batch of plain grilled chicken skewers before saucing, or brush the kids' portions with a mix of soy sauce and a little honey instead of the gochujang sauce, so they get the same smoky char without the heat.
nutritionNote: A protein-forward grilled dish; the sauce is high in sugar and sodium, so serve it on the side rather than fully coating every skewer, and pair with a vegetable banchan.
